content: Buruli ulcer is a severe necrotizing skin infection caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans, predominantly affecting individuals in tropical and subtropical regions. The disease typically begins as subcutaneous nodules and progresses to deep ulcers, often located on the limbs or face. If left untreated, it can result in permanent disfigurement and disability. Treatment generally involves antibiotics, sometimes in combination with surgery. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various drug treatments for Buruli ulcer. A comprehensive search of multiple databases and clinical trial registries was conducted up to December 19, 2017. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and prospective observational studies comparing antibiotic regimens, with or without surgery, were included. Data were extracted and analyzed using rigorous methods, including the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of evidence. A total of 18 studies were included: five RCTs with 319 participants and 13 observational studies with 1665 participants. These studies were conducted in regions with high Buruli ulcer prevalence, such as West Africa and Australia. Most studies evaluated combination antibiotic therapies, often alongside surgery. Only one RCT employed adequate methods to minimize bias. Monotherapy One RCT and one observational study assessed clofazimine, while another RCT evaluated sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim. These studies had small sample sizes and did not demonstrate significant treatment effects. Combination Therapy 1. Rifampicin with Streptomycin: One RCT and six observational studies evaluated this combination for treatment durations of 2, 4, 8, or 12 weeks (941 participants). The RCT, which was underpowered, did not show a significant difference in recurrence rates at 12 months when comparing the addition of antibiotics to surgery versus surgery alone (RR 0.12, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.51; very low-certainty evidence). Five single-arm observational studies (828 participants) using this regimen for eight weeks with surgery reported healing rates between 84.5% and 100%, assessed over six weeks to one year. Four observational studies evaluating this regimen without surgery reported healing rates ranging from 48% to 95%, assessed over eight weeks to one year. 2. Rifampicin with Clarithromycin: Two observational studies examined this combination. One study (30 participants) reported a 50% healing rate at 12 months when the regimen was used without surgery for eight weeks. Another study (21 participants) reported a 100% healing rate at 12 months when the regimen was used with surgery for varying durations. 3. Rifampicin with Streptomycin Initially, Followed by Rifampicin with Clarithromycin: One RCT compared this regimen (four weeks of each phase) to continuing rifampicin with streptomycin for eight weeks. All participants had small lesions, and healing rates exceeded 90% in both groups without surgery (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.03; 151 participants; low-certainty evidence). A single-arm observational study (41 participants) evaluated substituting streptomycin with clarithromycin in the consolidation phase (six weeks, total eight weeks) without surgery, reporting a 98% healing rate at 12 months. 4. Novel Combination Therapies: Two large prospective studies in Australia investigated novel regimens. One study (132 participants) evaluated rifampicin combined with ciprofloxacin, clarithromycin, or moxifloxacin without surgery, reporting a 76.5% healing rate at 12 months. Another study (90 participants) assessed combinations of two to three drugs (rifampicin, ciprofloxacin, clarithromycin, ethambutol, moxifloxacin, or amikacin) with surgery, reporting a 100% healing rate. Adverse Effects and Paradoxical Reactions Adverse effects were reported in three RCTs (158 participants) and eight observational studies (878 participants). These effects were consistent with the known safety profiles of the drugs. Paradoxical reactions, characterized by clinical worsening due to an enhanced immune response to M. ulcerans, were evaluated in six observational studies (822 participants), with incidence rates ranging from 1.9% to 26%. Conclusions While antibiotic combination therapies appear effective, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether any specific regimen is superior. The influence of lesion size, disease stage, and the need for surgery on treatment outcomes remains unclear. Future trials, particularly those involving clarithromycin with rifampicin and other novel regimens, should address these factors to optimize treatment strategies.
